title: Purity without hemlock
source_text: Οἱ δ᾿ ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐπὶ ἰδιωτείᾳ ἐξουθενούμενοι καὶ μωροὶ καὶ ἀνδράποδα εἶναι λεγόμενοι, κἂν μόνον πιστεύωσιν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ θεῷ. παραδεξάμενοι τὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίαν τοσοῦτον ἀποδέουσιν ἀσελγείας καὶ ἀκαθαρσίας καὶ πάσης τῆς ἐν συνουσίαις ἀσχημοσύνης, ὡς καὶ τρόπον τελείων ἱερέων, πᾶσαν συνουσίαν ἀποστραφέντων, πολλοὺς αὐτῶν παντελῶς καθαρεύειν, οὐ μόνον ἀπὸ πάσης μίξεως. καὶ εἷς μέν που παρ᾿ Ἀθηναίοις ἱεροφάντης, οὐδὲ πιστευόμενος ἑαυτοῦ τὰς ἀρσενικὰς ὀρέξεις ὡς κύριος αὐτῶν εἶναι δυνάμενος καὶ κρατεῖν αὐτῶν ἐς ὅσον βούλεται, κωνειασθεὶς τὰ ἄρσενα μέρη καθαρὸς εἶναι νομίζεται πρὸς τὴν νενομισμένην παρ᾿ Ἀθηναίοις ἁγιστείαν· ἔστι δ᾿ ἐν Χριστιανοῖς ἰδεῖν ἄνδρας μὴ δεηθέντας κωνείου, ἵνα τὸ θεῖον καθαρῶς θεραπεύσωσιν, ἀλλ᾿ ἀρκουμένους λόγῳ ἀντὶ κωνείου, ὡς πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν ἀπὸ τῆς διανοίας αὐτῶν ἐξελάσαντες τὸ θεῖον εὐχαῖς θεραπεύωσι. παρ᾿ ἄλλοις δὲ νομιζομένοις εἶναι θεοῖς παρθένοι πάνυ εὐαρίθμητοι, εἴτε ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων φρουρούμεναι εἴτε καὶ μὴ (οὐ γὰρ τοῦτο πρόκειται νῦν ἐξετάζειν). δοκοῦσι διατελεῖν ἐν τῇ διὰ τὴν εἰς τὸ θεῖον τιμὴν καθαρότητι· ἐν δὲ Χριστιανοῖς οὐ διὰ τὰς παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις τιμὰς, οὐ διὰ μισθοὺς καὶ ἀργύρια οὐδὲ διὰ δοξάριον ἀσκοῦσι τὴν παντελῆ παρθενίαν, καὶ ὡς „ἐδοκίμασαν τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει,“ τηροῦνται ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν δοκίμῳ νῷ καὶ τῷ „ποιεῖν τὰ“ „καθήκοντα,“ πληρούμεναι πάσης δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἀγαθότητος.
pass_a_gloss: But those despised (ἐξουθενέω) by them for unlearnedness (ἰδιωτεία) and said to be fools (μωροί) and slaves (ἀνδράποδα), if only they entrust (πιστεύω) themselves to God, having received the teaching of Jesus, fall so far short of (ἀποδέω) wantonness (ἀσέλγεια) and uncleanness (ἀκαθαρσία) and all indecency (ἀσχημοσύνη) in sexual unions (συνουσίαι), that, in the manner of perfect (τέλειος) priests (ἱερεῖς) who turned away from all intercourse (συνουσία), many of them are entirely pure (καθαρεύω), not only from all mixing/union (μίξις). And one hierophant (ἱεροφάντης) among the Athenians, not trusting himself as able to be master (κύριος) of his male desires (ὀρέξεις) and to control (κρατέω) them as far as he wishes, having been hemlocked (κωνειάω) in the male parts is thought (νομίζω) pure for the customary rite (ἁγιστεία) among the Athenians; but among Christians one can see men not needing hemlock (κώνειον) in order to serve (θεραπεύω) the divine (τὸ θεῖον) purely, but content (ἀρκέομαι) with the word/reason (λόγος) instead of hemlock, so that having driven out (ἐξελαύνω) every desire (ἐπιθυμία) from their mind (διάνοια) they serve the divine with prayers. Among others thought to be gods, virgins (παρθένοι) quite easily counted, whether guarded (φρουρέω) by men or not (for it is not set before us now to examine), seem to continue (διατελέω) in purity (καθαρότης) through honour (τιμή) toward the divine; but among Christians not for honours among men, not for wages (μισθοί) and silver (ἀργύρια) nor for a little glory (δοξάριον) they practise (ἀσκέω) complete virginity (παρθενία), and as 'they approved (δοκιμάζω) to have God in acknowledgement (ἐπίγνωσις)', they are kept (τηρέω) by God in an approved (δόκιμος) mind (νοῦς) and in 'doing the fitting things', being filled with all righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) and goodness (ἀγαθότης).
pass_b_english: But those whom they despise for lack of learning, and call fools and slaves, even if all they do is entrust themselves to God, have received the teaching of Jesus and stand so far from licentiousness and uncleanness and every indecency in sexual relations that many of them, after the manner of perfect priests who have turned away from all sexual intercourse, keep themselves wholly pure, and not only from every act of union.

At Athens, I suppose, there is one hierophant who, not trusting himself to be master of his male desires and able to control them as far as he wishes, has his male parts treated with hemlock, and is then thought pure for the worship that is customary among the Athenians. But among Christians one can see men who have had no need of hemlock in order to serve the Divine purely, but who are content with the word instead of hemlock, so that, having driven every desire out of their minds, they serve the Divine with prayers.

In the service of others who are reckoned to be gods there are virgins, very easily counted, whether they are guarded by men or not (for it is not our purpose now to examine that), who seem to remain in purity for the sake of the honour paid to the deity. But among Christians it is not for honours from men, not for wages and money, nor for a scrap of glory, that they practise perfect virginity; and as “they saw fit to keep God in their knowledge” (compare Romans 1:28), they are kept by God in an approved mind and in “doing what is fitting,” filled with all righteousness and goodness (compare Romans 1:28–29).

choices.choice: Origen turns Romans 1:28-29 into its opposite: Paul says ‘they did not see fit (οὐκ ἐδοκίμασαν) to keep God in knowledge’, so God gave them up to ‘an unapproved mind (ἀδόκιμον νοῦν)’, ‘to do what is not fitting (μὴ καθήκοντα)’, ‘filled with all unrighteousness’. Origen drops the negatives and applies the words to Christian virgins; the citations are therefore marked ‘compare’. ‘πληρούμεναι’ is feminine, so the subject of the last clause is the Christian virgins (women); English ‘they’ keeps this without adding a noun. ‘οὐ μόνον ἀπὸ πάσης μίξεως’ ends the sentence without its expected ‘but also’ clause; the sense is that their purity goes beyond bodily abstinence (developed in the next sentence about desire driven from the mind). Rendered ‘and not only from every act of union’; a lacuna is possible. ‘κἂν μόνον πιστεύωσιν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ θεῷ. παραδεξάμενοι’: the full stop in the source is misplaced; the participle belongs to the main verb ‘ἀποδέουσιν’. ‘λόγῳ ἀντὶ κωνείου’: ‘λόγος’ may mean the divine Word, the Christian teaching, or reason; rendered lowercase ‘the word’ to leave it open. ‘τὸ θεῖον’ rendered ‘the Divine’. The hierophant of Eleusis and the hemlock: a known ancient report, given here as Origen gives it; no classical source is cited inline. ‘κἂν μόνον πιστεύωσιν’ = ‘even if (καὶ ἐάν) they only entrust themselves’: the despised simple believers who have nothing but faith.

'if only they entrust themselves to God and receive the teaching of Jesus, are so far from' -> 'even if all they do is entrust themselves to God, have received the teaching of Jesus and stand so far from' (κἂν = 'even if', not 'provided that'; the participle παραδεξάμενοι goes with the main verb, as the note already said)
'Among others who are reckoned to be gods' -> 'In the service of others who are reckoned to be gods' (παρά + dative of the gods; old wording could read as 'among other people')
Kept the open 'not only from every act of union' (possible lacuna, noted); checked the reversed use of Romans 1:28-29, marked 'compare'

choices.choice: 7.48: 'οὐ μόνον ἀπὸ πάσης μίξεως' has no 'but also' clause, so a lacuna is possible. It is rendered literally and flagged in the note.
